## F1-P

Beat 1 — 17:20–17:28, ticket room (setup). Olin asks for the token, citing only "someone on the far bank." Neri wants an explanation and his approval but will not ask; her thumb rests on the token. The limit is on-page: one token, one person, consumed on boarding, no exception. Opening knowledge: his stated reason only. Commitment: she says she's crossing.

Beat 2 — 17:28–17:36, walk (resistance). Olin presses with a partial, unverifiable claim (the person is ill), unconfirmed by narration. Neri tests surrender, proof, refusal — and refuses; the apprenticeship is earned, the gate closes 17:55. Olin's agency: he chooses how much to reveal, stopping short of the truth.

Beat 3 — 17:36–17:40, landing (choice). Last call: custody never leaves Neri; the token is consumed at the gangway, 17:40. Olin's agency: he watches, chooses not to seize it — his constraint, not her force.

Beat 4 — 17:40–17:55, crossing, gate (outcome). The ferry runs 17:40–17:52; Neri reaches the gate at 17:54, one minute before close, claiming the apprenticeship. She accepts the limit: Olin does not cross; his motive stays unresolved; the estrangement stands. Payoff: the token she guarded, wanting his approval, is spent on herself — a door, not approval.

Author-planned motive, not opening knowledge: Olin is bound for their ill mother; he withholds it: Neri, knowing, would surrender it — wanted, unbearable.

## F1-D

The ticket room smelled of lamp oil and river cold. The counter clock said 17:20. Neri kept her right hand in her coat pocket, thumb hooked around the token. It had warmed to the shape of her pocket, the only thing in the room that mattered.

Olin stood by the counter, shoulders set, not looking at her. "I need your token."

"It's mine." Flatter than she meant. She wanted to ask why tonight, why him — but the question sat in her throat like a second token she could not spend.

"There's someone on the far bank," he said, to the counter, the lamp, wherever her eyes were. "I have to see them."

"Who?" The word slipped out before she could cage it.

Olin turned. His face did what it always did — it closed up, polite and unreachable. "You wouldn't know them."

"Then tell me."

"One trip. One." He held out his hand, palm up, patient as a man holding out a cup. "That's the whole of it."

At the counter, the clerk slid a paper ticket across the wood. Cold. Her token, in her pocket, was warm. Eight minutes to the landing, twelve across. The far-bank apprenticeship gate closed at 17:55, and the listing said, in small print, that the token admitted exactly one person, was consumed on boarding, and allowed no exception tonight. She had read it three times that morning, as if the paper might change.

"I earned that crossing," she said. Not to him — to the room, the lamp, the token.

Olin's hand was still out. "Let me be the one."

She looked at his palm. She thought of the eight-minute walk, of standing at the landing with time to board or to watch. She thought of every year of wanting the look he gave what he wanted.

Her fingers found the token through the wool. She pulled it out — warm, shaped by her pocket — and set it in his palm. His fingers closed; for a moment she imagined he might give it back.

He did not. He pocketed it and walked to the door. She did not follow. The lamp ticked. The river moved.

State delta: 17:27 — the token passes from Neri's right coat pocket to Olin's custody; Neri holds no crossing token, and her 17:55 apprenticeship gate is now unreachable tonight. Olin's true motive remains unknown.

## F2-P

Beat 1 — 12:00, doorway (setup). Rafi holds the only booth (key on the desk) to 12:20; his fifteen-minute audition take is due 12:30. Leena arrives with Pia, needing her own fifteen-minute violin take due 12:30. Twenty minutes, two fifteens, one booth — both cannot fit. Setup: she asks for the room, not Rafi; he wants to be asked for.

Beat 2 — 12:00–12:05, negotiation (resistance). Leena presses with a hopeful "half an hour"; narration won't endorse it. Pia offers to surrender her fifteen; Leena overrules. Leena's agency: she routes the request through Pia and withholds why she left the band. Rafi tests refusal — keep the key, start his take — flinching at Pia's face.

Beat 3 — 12:05, the choice. Rafi hands the key to Leena; Pia records 12:05–12:20, ending as the next group arrives. Rafi's audition is dead: no second booth, no remote, no extension — a concrete cost, his own.

Beat 4 — 12:20–12:30, outcome (payoff). Pia finishes; Leena submits by 12:30. Rafi records nothing, accepting the fixed limit. No reconciliation: she thanked the room, never him. Payoff: the want to be asked for lapses unpaid — the quiet minute is the asking that never came.

Author-planned motive, not opening knowledge: Leena left the band over envy of Rafi's break — unverified, never on-page; Rafi knows only that she left.

## F2-D

The key lay on the desk just inside the booth, beside a coffee ring from an earlier optimist. The clock said 12:00. Rafi had the room until 12:20 and needed fifteen uninterrupted minutes for an audition due at 12:30.

The door opened. Leena walked in with her daughter and no apology. The violin came in a case.

"Nice timing," Rafi said.

"Perfect timing," Leena said. "Pia needs fifteen minutes too, uninterrupted, also due at 12:30." She said it to the room, the booth, the twenty minutes he stood in. "This is the only booth."

Rafi looked at Pia. Pia looked at the floor, then at her case, then at the corner, as if it might have an opinion. She shifted her weight; the case stayed shut.

"So," Rafi said. "You want the room."

"I want the room," Leena said. "Just the room. Not forgiveness."

He heard it, the careful phrasing: rent the space without renting him. He wanted her to ask for him, and resented that he wanted it. He thought of the last gig of their old band, the one she never came to.

"I can start now," he said. "Get my fifteen in."

"And Pia?"

"Waits," he said. "Or Pia records after 12:20, when the next group has it. That's the arithmetic."

Pia's hands tightened on the case. "You sure?"

"She's sure," Leena said, not looking at him. "Home won't work."

Rafi picked up the key. It was heavier than it looked, or maybe that was the coffee ring. He thought about being useful only when needed, the whole history in one small brass key. Twenty minutes. Two fifteen-minute recordings. One booth.

He put the key in Leena's hand and stepped back.

"Start now," he said. "Pia gets the fifteen. Done by 12:20, when the next group gets the room — no slack, so play like the floor's on fire."

Leena took the key. She did not thank him — not for the room, not for anything. Pia went in and shut the door. The clock said 12:05. Rafi stood in the hallway: audition due 12:30, no booth, no remote, no extension, one quiet minute, nothing said.

State delta: 12:05 — the key passes from the desk to Rafi to Leena; Pia's take runs 12:05–12:20. Rafi records no audition take; his 12:30 audition goes unrecorded. No reconciliation occurs.
